criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Mission purpose, need, single-spacecraft choice with reasons, and user groups are all addressed with supporting context and some sourced statistics. The operator is not clearly identified, and the customer description is general. Funding discussion is speculative. Overall a solid, referenced introduction with minor gaps.

evidence.quote: Coral reefs, specifically the Great Barrier Reef, would immensely benefit from dedicated satellite monitoring.
Thus, only one satellite is required.
The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education.

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: All major segments are covered, with an orbit table, STK access data, ground track images and an EOL option. However, the altitude logic is contradictory, the Vega E is unflown yet is used without caveat, and the RAAN explanation is unjustified. The ground station is at about 42°S, not near the pole. There is little quantitative support for swath, resolution or EOL, and STK files are not evidenced.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: The conclusion summarises the configuration and notes launch-vehicle risk, which is useful. However, it does not restate key quantitative results such as the 97.79° inclination or the access statistics. Several claims are generic or overstated, such as bleaching being minimised or solved.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Sections follow a recognisable structure with headings and a contents list. Figures and tables are unnumbered and untitled, heading levels are inconsistent, and one sentence is broken. Launch-table superscripts cite [49]-[74], which are absent from the 10-item bibliography. [6] is Wikipedia, and [10] is used for two different sources.

technical_issues.issue: Altitude justification is inconsistent: a higher altitude gives lower resolution, yet this is called desirable. No swath or ground sample distance calculation supports the 600 km choice.
The claim that the initial RAAN indicates the launch facility location is unsupported and does not match standard orbit-element meaning.
Mt Pleasant (about 42°S) is described as selected for a latitude close to the poles, which is a weak and partly incorrect rationale.
The access table duplicates access 14 as access 15, and the statistics say 15 accesses while the list is labelled with a '----' row, so the count is inconsistent.
Vega E is used as the launch vehicle though not yet flown; its 2024 first-launch claim is unsourced and conflicts with the VV18 rideshare plan.
A sentence is truncated, and the drag-sail description is incomplete. The EOL strategy has no decay time or delta-V analysis despite stated STK runs to 2030.
The descending pass is described as constantly in sunlight, which overstates the sunlit conditions for a sun-synchronous orbit.
Wikipedia is cited as [6], which the brief prohibits. Launch-table citations [49]-[74] are not in the bibliography, and [10] is reused for two different sources.

overall: A broad, mostly complete space-segment design with appropriate STK support and a clear mission rationale. Weaknesses include contradictory altitude logic, an unflown launch vehicle, an access-table error, an incomplete EOL analysis, unnumbered figures and tables, and Wikipedia use with mismatched citations. Quantitative justification and reference integrity need substantial improvement.

feedback.summary: You have built a clear, mostly complete space-segment design for monitoring the Great Barrier Reef, with a well-motivated purpose and a sound single-satellite rationale. The main gaps are the quantitative justification of your orbit and launch choices, an inconsistent access table, an incomplete end-of-life analysis, and reference and figure presentation. Addressing these would raise several criteria by a level.
next_steps: Strengthen your orbit and launch justification with quantitative evidence: add a swath or ground sample distance calculation for 600 km, correct the RAAN explanation, and caveat or justify the unflown Vega E.
Complete your access and end-of-life analysis: correct the duplicated access entry and its statistics, and quantify your end-of-life option with a decay time or delta-V estimate.
Repair referencing and presentation: replace the Wikipedia source, reconcile citations [49]-[74] and the reused [10] with the bibliography, and number and title all figures and tables consistently.

criteria.C1: Your introduction clearly states the mission purpose (monitoring coral reefs, particularly the Great Barrier Reef), explains why it is needed, justifies using one satellite, and names likely users such as CSIRO and BOM. To reach Accomplished, clearly identify the operator, describe the customer groups in more specific detail, support the need with more referenced evidence, and remove speculative funding comments.
criteria.C2: You cover all required segments, including launch, the orbit table, STK access data, ground tracks and an end-of-life option. To reach Accomplished, support your key choices quantitatively. The 600 km altitude argument is contradictory (higher altitude lowers resolution yet is called desirable), so add swath or ground sample distance calculations. Correct the RAAN explanation, justify the ~42°S ground station, caveat the unflown Vega E, fix the sunlight claim for the descending pass, and quantify end-of-life.
criteria.C3: Your conclusion summarises the satellite configuration and usefully acknowledges launch-vehicle risk. To reach Accomplished, draw specific conclusions from your evidence: restate key results such as the 97.79° inclination and access statistics, and show how they support mission feasibility. Replace generic claims, such as coral bleaching being minimised or solved, with conclusions your analysis actually supports, and note the limits of your design.
criteria.C4: Your report has a recognisable structure, with headings and a contents list. To reach Accomplished, number and title every figure and table consistently, fix the truncated sentence and inconsistent heading levels, and correct the bibliography: replace the Wikipedia source [6], add the missing sources cited as [49]-[74], resolve the reused [10], and check that every in-text citation matches a reference. Proofread for spelling, grammar and formatting consistency.
